newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Aluminium in for better time - Aluvic.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Aluminium in for better time - Aluvic.

text.p: Following a tough period, most world aluminium markets are on the mend, Australia's Aluminium Smelters of Victoria Ltd (Aluvic) said on Wednesday.
"Very late last year, we saw the consumers come back reasonably strongly for the first time for about 12 months," Greg Turnidge, managing director of Aluvic, said in an interview.
Aluvic holds 25 percent of the Portland aluminium smelter in Victoria state and is owned by the state government.
Turnidge said stronger perceptions of economic growth and healthier order books for producers were underpinning brigher prospects for aluminium.

"We've seen a lot of the hesitancy that started to develop about the U.S. market late last year subside, and the potential for interest rate increases seems to have died away a little bit ... we're getting a lot of feedback out the U.S. market that order books are as strong as they've ever been," Turnidge said.
Turnidge said there was clear indication that stock building is occurring in the U.S. in anticipatiion of a strong 1997.
"We're also seeing coming out of Europe the same kind of noises for the first time in a few years ... in the form of consumer buying."
He said this suggested the worst of the European market for aluminium may be ending, with growth in consumption possibly averaging two to three percent this year.
"Those two things coming together are very important to swing the fundamental position of aluminium around," Turnidge said.
However, Japan, Aluvic's major market, remains the wildcard, Turnidge said.

While demand has shown to be steady, a possible 300,000 tonnes waiting to be imported on April 1 under Japan's General Systems of Preference (GSP) tariff exemption scheme could curb future demand, Turnidge said.
"There's a lot of talk in Japan that there's been an inventory build-up in anticipation of the sales tax adjustment that is occuring on April 1," he said.
As a result, there has been significant forward buying of aluminium in late 1996 and early this year in anticipation of the surge, he said.
Turnidge said he expects aluminium prices to average around US$1,650-$1,700 a tonne this year versus a 1996 average of about US$1,500.
But the rally still could be short-lived as new production facilities start to come on line, starting in the latter half of this year, adding to the global supply stream, he said.
"We're not sure how sustained the price recovery will be," Turnidge said.
Current premiums for aluminium were running at about US$120 a tonne in the U.S., down from US$140 recently. In Japan, premiums have increased to around US$85 a tonne from about US$75, Turnidge said.
The Portland smelter produces about 294,000 tonnes of aluminium a year, about 30,000 tonnes below capacity due to ongoing negotiations with the Victorian state government over additional power.
An agreement could lead to privatisation of Aluvic and an expansion of production, Turnidge said.
"We'd very much like to see Portland grow," he said.
Aluvic also is looking outside of smelting and is active in supplying value-added aluminium aerospace components to aircraft manufacturers in Europe and the U.S.

Turnidge also said active hedging programmes for both aluminium and in currency markets has enabled operations to better weather last year's 16 percent fall in alumnium prices and unfavourable movements in the Australian dollar.

Aluvic has managed to keep its achieved exchange rate between 68 and 69 U.S. cents to the Australian dollar versus spot rates that have risen steadily to over 79 U.S. cents in the second half of 1996 from under 74 cents in the first half,
Turnidge said.
The other Portland joint venturers are Alcoa of Australia percent, China International Trust and Investment Corp 10 percent and Eastern Aluminium 10 percent.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
